description: An interface maintaining a sequence of items where order is extrinsic, supporting build/len, static get_at/set_at, and dynamic insert/delete operations at either end or a given index.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Maintain a sequence of items (order is extrinsic)

description: An interface maintaining a set of items with unique keys, where order is intrinsic (by key); supports build/len, find, insert/delete, and Order operations. A dictionary is a Set without the Order operations.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Sequence about extrinsic order, set is about intrinsic order

description: A Sequence implementation giving Theta(1) get_at/set_at, but Theta(n) dynamic insert/delete because of reallocation and shifting.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Array is great for static operations! get_at(i) and set_at(i, x) in Theta(1) time!

description: A pointer-based Sequence where each node stores an item and a pointer to the next node; insert/delete from the front run in Theta(1) time, but get_at/set_at cost Theta(n).

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Can now insert and delete from the front in Theta(1) time! Yay!

description: A Sequence that allocates extra space at a chosen fill ratio so reallocation doesn't happen on every dynamic operation, giving Theta(1) amortized cost for last-position insert/delete.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Allocate extra space so reallocation does not occur with every dynamic operation

description: An analysis technique distributing cost over many operations: an operation has amortized cost T(n) if any k operations cost at most k*T(n) total, even if individual operations occasionally cost more.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Operation has amortized cost T(n) if k operations cost at most <= kT(n)

description: A pointer-based data structure with three pointers per node (item, parent, left, right), designed so operations run in O(h) time for root height h.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Binary tree is pointer-based data structure with three pointers per node

description: The inherent order of a binary tree's nodes: every node in a node's left subtree comes before it, every node in its right subtree comes after.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: A binary tree has an inherent order: its traversal order

description: depth(X) is the length of the path from node X to the root; height(X) is the max depth of any node in the subtree rooted at X. Tree operations are designed to run in O(h) time.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Idea: Design operations to run in O(h) time for root height h, and maintain h = O(log n)

description: A binary tree whose traversal order equals sorted key order, equivalently: for every node, every key in its left subtree is <= its key <= every key in its right subtree.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Set Binary Tree (a.k.a. Binary Search Tree / BST): Traversal order is sorted order increasing by key

description: Maintaining a node.size field at each binary tree node, updated in O(h) time per insert/delete, so a subtree's size can be checked in O(1) time -- used to implement Sequence-style subtree_at(i).

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Maintain the size of each node's subtree at the node via augmentation

description: Finding the next (or previous) node in a binary tree's traversal order: if X has a right child, its successor is the first node of the right subtree; otherwise it is the lowest ancestor for which X is in its left subtree.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Find successor of node <X> in the traversal order (predecessor is symmetric)

description: A Set interface optimized for build, insert, delete_max, and find_max -- keeping track of many items and quickly accessing/removing the most important one.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Order items by key = priority so Set interface (not Sequence interface)

aliases: array as a complete binary tree
description: Interpreting an array as a complete binary tree with no stored pointers, using index arithmetic (left(i)=2i+1, right(i)=2i+2, parent(i)=floor((i-1)/2)) to compute neighbors.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Complete binary tree structure can be implicit instead of storing pointers

description: At node i, Q[i] >= Q[j] for j in {left(i), right(i)}. A max-heap satisfies this at every node, which implies every node is >= all nodes in its subtree, so the maximum item is always at the root.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Max-Heap Property at node i: Q[i] >= Q[j] for j in {left(i), right(i)}

description: Append the new item to the end of the array, then swap with its parent repeatedly until the Max-Heap Property holds. Running time Theta(log n).

sourceAnchors.excerpt: max_heapify_up(i): swap with parent until Max-Heap Property

description: Swap the root with the last item, remove the last item, then swap the new root down with its larger child repeatedly until the Max-Heap Property holds. Running time Theta(log n).

sourceAnchors.excerpt: max_heapify_down(i): swap root with larger child until Max-Heap Property

description: The sorting algorithm produced by plugging a binary max-heap into priority queue sort (build, then repeatedly delete_max), running in O(n log n) time, in-place.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Plugging max-heap into priority queue sort gives us a new sorting algorithm

description: Building a heap by treating the full array as a complete tree from the start and calling max_heapify_down from the last index down to the first (leaves-up), which costs O(n) total rather than the Omega(n log n) of repeated inserts.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Idea! Treat full array as a complete binary tree from start, then max_heapify_down(i) for i from n-1 to 0

description: A set of vertices V and a set of pairs of vertices E, either directed (ordered pairs) or undirected (unordered pairs); this course assumes simple graphs.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices V and a set of pairs of vertices E

description: Storing a graph as a Set structure mapping each vertex u to Adj(u), itself stored as an array or linked list, giving Theta(|V|+|E|) space and defining 'linear time' for graph algorithms.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: for each u, need to store Adj(u) in another data structure called an adjacency list

description: A path is a sequence of vertices connected by edges; distance delta(u,v) is the length of the shortest path from u to v, defined as infinity if v is unreachable.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: The distance delta(u, v) from u to v is the minimum length of any path from u to v

description: Rather than returning every full shortest path, store each vertex's parent P(v) -- the second-to-last vertex on a shortest path from s -- forming a tree of size O(|V|).

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Set of parents comprise a shortest paths tree with O(|V|) size!

description: Explores graph nodes in increasing order of distance from a source, computing level sets L_i, and runs in O(|V|+|E|) time -- solves Single Source Shortest Paths.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Idea! Explore graph nodes in increasing order of distance
Breadth-First Search (BFS) - algorithm that solves Single Source Shortest Paths

description: L_i is the set of all vertices at distance i from the BFS source; BFS computes each L_i from L_{i-1} by examining every neighbor of every vertex in L_{i-1} not already placed at an earlier level.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Goal: Compute level sets L_i = {v | v in V and d(s, v) = i}

description: Visits outgoing adjacencies recursively, never revisiting a vertex, following any path until stuck then backtracking; solves Single Source Reachability in O(|E|) time.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Idea! Visit outgoing adjacencies recursively, but never revisit a vertex

description: Repeating a search algorithm A on any unvisited vertex until all vertices have been visited, to explore an entire graph rather than just vertices reachable from one source; runs in O(|V|+|E|) time.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Repeat the following until all vertices have been visited: Choose an arbitrary unvisited vertex s

description: A partition of an undirected graph's vertices into subsets that are each internally connected with no edges between different subsets.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Connected_Components(G): given undirected graph G = (V, E), return partition of V into subsets

description: An ordering f on the vertices of a DAG such that every edge (u,v) satisfies f(u) < f(v); the reverse of a Full-DFS finishing order is a topological order.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: Claim: If G = (V, E) is a DAG, the reverse of a finishing order is a topological order

description: Checking whether a graph is acyclic by testing whether the reverse finishing order of Full-DFS is a valid topological order; if not, DFS traversed an edge from a vertex to one of its own ancestors.

sourceAnchors.excerpt: If reverse finishing order for Full-DFS is not a topological order, then G must contain a cycle
